title: Transfers of energy and matter
summary: How energy flows through ecosystems and is lost as heat at each trophic level, while carbon and other elements are recycled, and how human activity is shifting the carbon cycle.

keyterms.definition: A system, such as an ecosystem, in which both energy and matter can enter and exit.
An organism that makes its own carbon compounds from simple inorganic substances using an external energy source (light or chemical oxidation).
An autotroph that obtains energy by oxidising inorganic substances, e.g. iron-oxidizing bacteria oxidising Fe²⁺ ions.
An organism that obtains carbon compounds from other organisms and uses them to build the carbon compounds it needs.
An organism, such as a saprotrophic fungus or bacterium, that obtains carbon compounds from dead organic matter, recycling nutrients.
The position of an organism in a food chain: producer, primary consumer, secondary consumer, tertiary consumer.
A diagram of interconnected food chains in an ecosystem; arrows show the direction of energy transfer from food to feeder.
A diagram showing the energy flowing through each trophic level per unit area per unit time, e.g. kJ m⁻² year⁻¹.
Accumulation of carbon compounds in biomass by autotrophs, measured in mass of carbon per unit area per unit time.
Accumulation of carbon compounds in biomass by heterotrophs; always lower than primary production.
An ecosystem or reservoir in which carbon uptake by photosynthesis exceeds release by respiration, e.g. a growing forest or peat bog.
An ecosystem or process that releases more carbon dioxide than it absorbs, e.g. a burning forest.
The record of atmospheric CO2 concentration at Mauna Loa since 1958, showing annual fluctuations and a long-term rise.

questions.prompt: Why are ecosystems described as open systems?
options: Both energy and matter can enter and exit
Neither energy nor matter can cross their boundaries
questions.explanation: Energy enters as light and leaves as heat, and matter can also move in or out, e.g. through migration, rivers or wind.

questions.statement: Sunlight is the main source of energy for most ecosystems.
questions.explanation: Photoautotrophs capture light energy, and almost all other organisms depend on them. A few ecosystems, such as those around deep-sea vents, rely on chemoautotrophs.

questions.prompt: How do iron-oxidizing bacteria obtain energy?
questions.explanation: They are chemoautotrophs: energy from oxidising inorganic substances is used to make carbon compounds from carbon dioxide.

questions.text: Organisms that make carbon compounds from simple inorganic substances using an external energy source are ___.
questions.explanation: Autotrophs use light (photoautotrophs) or chemical oxidation (chemoautotrophs) as their energy source to fix carbon.

questions.prompt: Match each type of organism to how it obtains energy or carbon compounds.

pairs.right: Uses light energy to make carbon compounds
Obtains carbon compounds from other organisms

questions.explanation: Autotrophs make their own carbon compounds; heterotrophs, including consumers and decomposers, depend on carbon compounds made by other organisms.

questions.prompt: Put this food chain in the order of energy flow.
questions.explanation: Chemical energy flows from the producer (grass) to the primary consumer, then the secondary and tertiary consumers.

questions.statement: In a food chain, arrows point from the consumer to the organism it eats.
questions.explanation: Arrows show the direction of energy transfer, so they point from the organism eaten to the organism that eats it.

questions.prompt: How do heterotrophs obtain the carbon compounds they need?
options: They digest carbon compounds from other organisms and use them to build their own
They fix carbon dioxide using light
They absorb carbon dioxide and convert it to proteins
They oxidise iron to make glucose
questions.explanation: Heterotrophs take in carbon compounds made by other organisms, digest them, and use the products to make their own carbon compounds, such as proteins.

questions.text: Organisms release the energy in carbon compounds by oxidising them in cell ___.
questions.explanation: Cell respiration oxidises carbon compounds such as glucose, releasing energy to make ATP; much of the energy is lost as heat.

questions.prompt: Why can energy not be recycled in an ecosystem, unlike chemical elements?
options: Energy is destroyed at each trophic level
Energy is converted to heat, which organisms cannot convert back into chemical energy
Decomposers lock energy into soil permanently
questions.explanation: Energy is not destroyed, but heat released by respiration is lost from the ecosystem; ecosystems therefore need a continuous input of energy, usually sunlight.

questions.prompt: In the food chain grass → grasshopper → frog, what trophic level is the frog?
questions.explanation: The grass is the producer, the grasshopper is the primary consumer, so the frog, which eats the grasshopper, is the secondary consumer.

questions.statement: In a pyramid of energy, each level is always narrower than the level below it.
questions.explanation: Energy is lost at every transfer, so less energy flows through each successive trophic level; energy pyramids cannot be inverted.

questions.prompt: Producers fix 10 000 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹ and primary consumers obtain 1000 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹. What is the efficiency of energy transfer?
questions.explanation: Efficiency = 1000 ÷ 10 000 × 100 = 10%. About 90% is lost, mostly as heat from respiration and in material not eaten or not digested.

questions.text: Most energy is lost between trophic levels as ___ released by cell respiration.
questions.explanation: Converting chemical energy to ATP in respiration and then using it is inefficient, so much energy is released as heat and lost from the ecosystem.

questions.prompt: Match each cause of energy loss between trophic levels to an example.

pairs.left: Not all of an organism is eaten
pairs.right: Roots, bones or fur left uneaten

questions.explanation: Only energy stored in new biomass of the consumer is available to the next trophic level; these losses explain why that is usually only about 10%.

questions.prompt: Why do food chains rarely have more than four or five trophic levels?
options: So little energy remains after successive losses that another level cannot be supported
Top predators cannot find enough prey because they are too large
Decomposers remove energy from the top levels
questions.explanation: With roughly 90% lost at each step, after a few levels there is too little energy to sustain a viable population of another consumer.

questions.text: Accumulation of carbon compounds in biomass by autotrophs is called ___ production.
questions.explanation: Primary production is carried out by autotrophs; secondary production is the accumulation of biomass by heterotrophs.

questions.prompt: Which biome usually has the highest primary production per unit area?
questions.explanation: High light intensity, warm temperatures and plentiful water all year allow high rates of photosynthesis. Deserts are limited by water; tundra by temperature and light.

questions.statement: Secondary production is usually greater than primary production in the same ecosystem.
questions.explanation: Secondary production is always lower, because heterotrophs depend on autotroph biomass and energy is lost at each transfer.

questions.prompt: Put the levels of a pyramid of energy in order, from base to top.
questions.explanation: Producers form the base with the most energy; each higher level has less energy available, so the bars become narrower.

questions.prompt: Match each process to its effect in the carbon cycle.

pairs.right: Converts atmospheric CO2 into carbon compounds
Releases CO2 from carbon compounds in organisms
Burning biomass or fossil fuels releases CO2
Passes carbon compounds along food chains

questions.explanation: Carbon cycles between the atmosphere and organisms; combustion of biomass, peat and fossil fuels adds extra CO2 to the atmosphere.

questions.prompt: When does an ecosystem act as a carbon sink?
options: When carbon uptake by photosynthesis exceeds carbon release by respiration
questions.explanation: A sink takes in more carbon than it releases, so carbon accumulates, e.g. in a growing forest or in peat where waterlogging slows decomposition.

questions.statement: An ecosystem acts as a carbon source when it releases more carbon dioxide than it absorbs.
questions.explanation: For example, a forest that is burned, or drained peatland that decomposes, releases more CO2 than is fixed by photosynthesis.

questions.prompt: Why does the Keeling curve show a fall in CO2 concentration each northern summer?
options: Combustion of fossil fuels stops in summer
Photosynthesis exceeds respiration in the large land area of the Northern Hemisphere
questions.explanation: In the northern summer, forests and crops photosynthesise rapidly and absorb more CO2 than is released; in winter, respiration exceeds photosynthesis and CO2 rises.

questions.text: The record of atmospheric CO2 measured at Mauna Loa since 1958 is called the ___ curve.
questions.explanation: The Keeling curve shows both annual fluctuations (seasonal photosynthesis) and a long-term upward trend (combustion of fossil fuels and biomass).

questions.prompt: What is the main cause of the long-term rise in the Keeling curve?
options: Combustion of fossil fuels and biomass
questions.explanation: Burning coal, oil, natural gas, peat and biomass releases carbon that had been locked away, adding CO2 faster than sinks can absorb it.

questions.statement: Burning coal, oil and natural gas does not affect atmospheric CO2, because their carbon originally came from the atmosphere.
questions.explanation: That carbon was removed from the cycle for millions of years; releasing it quickly adds CO2 to the atmosphere faster than it can be reabsorbed.

questions.prompt: How are photosynthesis and aerobic respiration interdependent?
options: Aerobic respiration depends on O2 from photosynthesis, and photosynthesis uses CO2 released by respiration
questions.explanation: Atmospheric oxygen comes from photosynthesis, and respiration returns CO2 that photosynthesis needs, linking the two processes globally.

questions.text: Unlike energy, chemical elements such as carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus are ___ within ecosystems.
questions.explanation: Energy flows through ecosystems and is lost as heat, but all the chemical elements organisms need are recycled between organisms and the environment.

questions.prompt: What is the role of decomposers in recycling elements?
options: They fix nitrogen gas into proteins
They release elements from dead organic matter, making them available to producers again
They convert heat back into chemical energy
They store carbon permanently in their cells
questions.explanation: Saprotrophs digest dead organic matter and release inorganic nutrients and CO2, so elements return to the soil and atmosphere for producers to reuse.
